dabhol: Dabhol, also written Dabul, is a small seaport town in the Ratnagiri district of Maharashtra. It lies on the northern and southern sides of the Vashishti River, which also flows by the town of Chiplun. Under the Bahmani dynasty the port was known as Mustafabad and later as Hamjabad before it took its present name. From the 14th to the 16th century it was the principal port of the southern Konkan, trading with ports of the Mediterranean Sea, the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf.

The Russian traveller Afanasy Nikitin, who visited India from 1468 to 1474, found Dabhol a large town and extensive seaport, to which horses from Mysore, Arabia and Khorasan were brought for sale, and which had links with all the major ports from India to Ethiopia. In the 15th and 16th centuries it was an opulent Muslim trading centre, first under the Bahmani sultans and later under those of Bijapur. It was the port with the most convenient access to the Bahmani capital at Bidar, and its fortunes rose with that dynasty; at its height it was arguably the most important port between Chaul and Goa.

That prominence made it a target. In December 1508 a Portuguese expeditionary force under Francisco de Almeida bombarded, sacked and razed the town in the Battle of Dabul, a prelude to the Battle of Diu, though the fort was not taken. The Portuguese tried several more times over the following decades to destroy it; at the last recorded attack, in 1571, the governor was Khwaja Ali Shirazi, and 150 men were killed at Dabhol.

The break-up of the Bahmani state into smaller Deccan sultanates hastened the port's decline. As new capitals were built its position was no longer so favourable, and during the 16th century much commerce moved south to the rising port of Rajapur. Shivaji conquered Dabhol around 1660 and annexed it to the new Maratha kingdom. It passed to Sambhaji, who gave it to Khando Ballal Chitnis as a reward for saving him from drowning in a river in Goa.

The Dabhol vatan is still claimed by descendants of the Chitnis family of Satara, although some descendants of the Shirke family argue that it should be theirs. On the southern side of the town, between the villages of Veldur and Ranavi, stands the Dabhol LNG power plant, which was set up by the company Enron.
dagestan: Dagestan lies in the North Caucasus along the western shore of the Caspian Sea, with about 405 kilometres of coastline. Most of it is mountainous, with the Greater Caucasus covering the south, where the highest point is the peak of Bazardüzü, on the border with Azerbaijan. The name means land of the mountains, from the Turkic word dağ, mountain, and the Persian suffix -stan, land. Because the terrain impedes travel and communication, the region is unusually diverse, with more than 30 local languages, most of them of the Nakh-Daghestanian family.

In the first centuries CE Caucasian Albania, which covered what is now Azerbaijan and southern Dagestan, became subordinate to the Parthian Empire and then a province of the Sasanian Empire. By the 6th century the Sasanian rulers had built a strong citadel at Derbent, known as the Caspian Gates. After the Arab conquest of 643 the people of the Derbent region became the first in what is now Russian territory to adopt Islam, and it spread from the towns into the highlands. The Mongols conquered Derbent between 1236 and 1239, and the Timurids followed.

In the early 16th century the Safavids reconsolidated Persian rule, which lasted intermittently until the early 19th century. In the 16th and 17th centuries legal traditions were codified, and mountain communities called djamaats won considerable autonomy. The Ottoman Empire held Dagestan between 1578 and 1606.Persia ceded southern Dagestan to Russia in the Treaty of Gulistan of 1813, and the Treaty of Turkmenchay of 1828 consolidated Russian control.

Heavy taxation, expropriation of estates and the building of fortresses, among them Makhachkala, provoked the highlanders to rise under the Imamate of Dagestan, led by Ghazi Mohammed, Hamzat Bek and Shamil, who led it from 1834 to 1859. The Caucasian War lasted until 1864. After the Bolshevik Revolution and years of fighting, the Dagestan Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was proclaimed on 20 January 1921.

Dagestan is a republic of Russia with its capital and largest city at Makhachkala, and its main towns include Derbent. It has over 3.1 million inhabitants, and Russian is the lingua franca although 14 languages are official. Most of its people are Sunni Muslims of the Shafii school, while the Caspian coast around Derbent has a Shia population. Its Sufi traditions go back to the 14th century, and Derbent, with its Sasanian citadel, remains its oldest city.
dakshinapatha: The name joins two Sanskrit words, dakshina, south, and patha, road. The later Vedic texts divide the Indian subcontinent into three parts: Aryavarta in the north, Madhya Desha in the centre and Dakshinapatha in the south. The Aitareya Brahmana, of the first half of the first millennium BCE, names peoples of the south of Vindhyan and north Deccan origin, among them the Satvants, Vidarbha, Andhra, Nishadas and Kuntis. The grammarian Panini, about 500 BCE, mentions the Asmaka Kingdom in connection with the south and with Kalinga.

The term has carried three meanings. It can denote the ancient south of the subcontinent below Uttarapatha, usually the Deccan and sometimes Tamilakam and Ceylon as well. It can mean the great southern highway, running from Magadha to Pratishthana. It has also been used for a kingdom on the Godavari River. The Junagarh rock inscription of 150 CE, set up by an Indo-Scythian king, records that he twice defeated Satakarni, the lord of Dakshinapatha, in fair fight and did not destroy him because of the nearness of their connection.

The southern road was one of two great highways that have linked the parts of the subcontinent since the Iron Age. The other, the Uttarapatha or great northern road, ran from Taxila through the Punjab to the Yamuna and followed that river south to Mathura; from there a route went on to Ujjain in Malwa and to Broach on the western coast. According to the writer Sanjeev Sanyal, the course of the northern road has stayed roughly the same since before the Mauryas, while the southern road appears to have drifted.

The route of Rama into exile in the epic may reflect an early version of it. By the time of the Buddha it started at Varanasi and ran through Vidisha in central India to Pratishthana, now Paithan, and it probably extended to the Chola, Chera and Pandya kingdoms of the far south. By the Mauryan period there would have been a branch from Ujjain to the ports of Gujarat, which made Ujjain a major city by the Gupta era. The modern highway that roughly corresponds to it runs much further east than the old road but still meets the northern road at Varanasi.
damascus: Damascus stands in south-western Syria on a plateau 680 metres above sea level, about 80 kilometres inland from the Mediterranean and sheltered by the Anti-Lebanon Mountains, which block rain from the sea. The Barada River, fed by mountain streams of melting snow, supplies the city with water, and the Ghouta, an irrigated belt of farmland, has produced vegetables, cereals and fruit since ancient times. The site lay at a crossroads of the north–south route linking Egypt with Asia Minor and the east–west desert route linking Lebanon with the Euphrates valley.

The name first appears as tjmsqw in a list of places of the Egyptian king Thutmose III, in the 15th century BCE, and as Dimašqa in the Amarna letters; its origin is uncertain. Greek myths gave three explanations of the Greek form Damaskós, among them a founder named Damaskos, a son of Hermes.

Radiocarbon dating at Tell Ramad, on the outskirts, suggests occupation possibly from around 6300 BCE, and settlement in the wider Barada basin goes back to 9000 BCE, though no large settlement stood within the city's later walls until the second millennium BCE. The Amarna letters of about 1350 BCE name Biryawaza as its ruler. Around 1260 BCE the region was a battleground between the Hittites and the Egyptians, and under a treaty between Hattusili III and Ramesses II control of the Damascus area passed to Egypt in 1259 BCE. After the Sea Peoples arrived around 1200 BCE, Damascus emerged as an influential centre, and from the 11th to the 7th century BCE it was the hub of an Aramaic kingdom.

Damascus was the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate from 661 to 750. When the Abbasid dynasty won, the seat of Islamic power moved to Baghdad and the city's importance declined. It regained significance in the Ayyubid, Mamluk and Ottoman periods.

Damascus is the capital of Syria and the seat of its central government, with a metropolitan area that includes Douma, Harasta, Darayya and Jaramana. The Ancient City of Damascus was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1979 and holds over 125 cultural heritage sites from the Hellenistic, Roman, Byzantine, Islamic and Ottoman periods; the best known of its more than 200 mosques is the Umayyad Mosque. Damascus University is the oldest and largest university in Syria.
dante-alighieri: Dante was born in Florence, probably around May 1265, a date deduced from allusions in the Divine Comedy. His father, Alighiero di Bellincione, was a businessman and moneylender, and his mother Bella, probably of the noble Abati family, died before he was ten. Dante claimed descent from the ancient Romans, but the earliest relative he could name was his great-great-grandfather Cacciaguida degli Elisei. His family was loyal to the Guelphs, who supported the papacy, against the Ghibellines, who supported the Holy Roman Empire.

Dante fought with the Florentine Guelphs at the Battle of Campaldino on 11 June 1289 and joined the Guild of Physicians and Apothecaries around 1295, which allowed him to hold public office. After the Guelphs defeated the Ghibellines they split into the White Guelphs, Dante's party, led by Vieri dei Cerchi, and the Black Guelphs, led by Corso Donati. The Whites wanted more freedom from Rome. In 1301 a delegation including Dante went to persuade Pope Boniface VIII not to send Charles of Valois to Florence, but the Pope kept Dante in Rome.

On 1 November 1301 Charles of Valois entered Florence with the Black Guelphs, who destroyed much of the city. In March 1302 Dante was condemned to exile for two years and a large fine, accused of corruption during his two months as prior in 1300. He did not pay and was condemned to perpetual exile, with the threat of being burned at the stake if he returned. He was a guest of Moroello Malaspina in Lunigiana in 1306–07, and in 1318 Guido II da Polenta invited him to Ravenna.

Dante died in Ravenna on 14 September 1321, aged about 56, of quartan malaria contracted while returning from a diplomatic mission to Venice. He was buried at the Church of San Pier Maggiore, later the Basilica di San Francesco. In 1329 Cardinal Bertrand du Pouget classified his Monarchia as heretical and sought to have his bones burned, but allies interceded. Florence built a tomb for him in Santa Croce in 1829, which has stayed empty, and in 2008 its city council rescinded his sentence.

Most of his work was composed after his exile. La Vita Nuova, the story of his love for Beatrice Portinari in poems and prose, is the only major work that predates it. The Divine Comedy describes a journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise, guided first by Virgil and then by Beatrice. He wrote it in Tuscan rather than Latin, and his use of the Florentine dialect helped establish standardised Italian. His De vulgari eloquentia was one of the first scholarly defences of the vernacular. Giovanni Boccaccio wrote the first formal biography.
danube: The Danube is the second-longest river in Europe after the Volga. It rises in the Black Forest of Germany, where the Brigach and the Breg meet at Donaueschingen, and flows southeast through four capital cities, Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade, before emptying into the Black Sea through the Danube Delta in Romania and Ukraine. Its drainage basin covers 817,000 square kilometres. Since ancient times it has been a traditional trade route.

The ancient Greeks called it the Istros, from a root possibly related to words for swift. Its Thraco-Phrygian name was Matoas, the bringer of luck, and the modern languages of the basin use names derived from the Latin Danubius. Geologically it is much older than the Rhine: before the last ice age the waters from the Alps now feeding the Rhine were carried east by the Urdonau, or original Danube.

The Danube basin was the site of some of the earliest human cultures, among them the Linear Pottery cultures and, from the sixth to third millennium BCE, the Vinča culture. The Vučedol culture of the third millennium BCE is known for its ceramics. Darius the Great of Persia crossed the river in the late 6th century BCE to subdue the Scythians, and in 336 BCE Alexander the Great advanced from Macedonia as far as the Danube and defeated the Triballian king Syrmus. The river was long a frontier of the Roman Empire. The Paris Conferences of 1856 and 1921 established an international regime to safeguard free navigation, and the Danube Commission was set up by seven riparian countries in 1948.

The Danube passes through or borders ten countries. Since the Rhine-Main-Danube Canal was completed in 1992 it has been part of a waterway of about 3,500 kilometres from Rotterdam on the North Sea to Sulina on the Black Sea. It supplies drinking water to about 20 million people and is an important source of hydropower. The Danube Delta is the largest river delta in the European Union and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. Johann Strauss's waltz The Blue Danube made the river's name known worldwide.
dara-shikoh: Muhammad Dara Shikoh was born at Ajmer on 20 March 1615, the first son and third child of Prince Khurram, the later Shah Jahan, and Mumtaz Mahal. He studied the Quran, history, Persian poetry and calligraphy, and beside his native Persian learned Hindi, Arabic and later Sanskrit. He and his elder sister Jahanara Begum were their father's favourite children.

On 1 February 1633 he married his half-cousin Nadira Banu Begum at Agra, and he contracted no other marriage. In the same year he was appointed heir apparent, which Shah Jahan formally confirmed on 10 September 1642 with the title Shahzada-e-Buland Iqbal, Prince of High Fortune. He was made governor of Allahabad in 1645 and of Gujarat in 1648.

Dara followed the Qadiri Sufi saint Mian Mir of Lahore, to whom Mullah Shah Badakhshi introduced him, and the mystic Sarmad Kashani, and he formed a friendship with the seventh Sikh Guru, Guru Har Rai. The treatise known as Majma-ul-Bahrain was written in Persian in 1654–55. His Persian version of fifty Upanishads, completed in 1657 and often called Sirr-i-Akbar, proposes in its introduction that the hidden book named in the Quran is the Upanishads. Annemarie Schimmel notes that he remained committed to the fundamentals of Islam and repeatedly called himself a Hanafi Qadiri.

He was a patron of painting, music and dancing, tastes that Aurangzeb frowned upon. The album of paintings and calligraphy that bears his name was presented to his wife in 1641–42; after her death the inscriptions linking it to him were deliberately erased.

After Samugarh he retreated by Delhi, Lahore, Multan and Thatta to Kathiawar, where Shah Nawaz Khan, governor of Gujarat, helped him raise a new army. After the rout at Deorai on 11 March 1659 he sought refuge in Sindh with the Afghan chieftain Malik Jeevan, whose life he had saved more than once, but Malik Jeevan seized him and informed Aurangzeb, whose army took him on 10 June 1659.

In Delhi he was paraded through the streets in chains on an elephant. A convocation of nobles and clergy called by Aurangzeb declared him a threat to the public peace and an apostate from Islam, and he was killed in front of his son on the night of 30 August 1659. He was buried in an unidentified grave in Humayun's tomb. In 2020 Sanjeev Kumar Singh, a municipal engineer, identified one of three unmarked cenotaphs beneath the dome as his, relying on the Alamgirnama; several historians and archaeologists have accepted the identification.
dead-sea: The Dead Sea is an endorheic lake with no outlet streams, and its main tributary is the Jordan River. It lies in the Jordan Rift Valley, formed by the Dead Sea Transform, a fault along the boundary between the African Plate and the Arabian Plate. In the late Pliocene and early Pleistocene the valley was repeatedly flooded from the Mediterranean, forming the Sedom Lagoon, which deposited rock salt up to 2.3 km thick. As the climate became more arid, Lake Lisan shrank and grew saltier, leaving the Dead Sea as its last remainder.

Historical English names include the Salt Sea, the Lake of Sodom, from the biblical account of its destruction, and Lake Asphaltites, from Greek and Latin. The Hebrew Bible records dwelling in caves near the sea before the Israelites came to Canaan and extensively in the time of King David. Greek and Jewish writers report that the Nabateans held a monopoly over the sea. The sixth-century Madaba Map indicates that trade across it was prevalent in the Byzantine period, and Greek Orthodox monks settled in the remote region, where Mar Saba is still a place of pilgrimage.

The Jewish village of Ein Gedi, inhabited continuously since the 5th century BCE, was destroyed by fire in the 7th century. From the seventh century the area declined and its population fell. Sugarcane was grown near the shores from the Crusader period and reached its peak under the Mamluks. Christopher Costigan explored the Jordan and the Dead Sea by boat in 1835, followed by Thomas Howard Molyneux in 1847, William Francis Lynch in 1848 and John MacGregor in 1869.

The Dead Sea lies between Jordan to the east and the West Bank and Israel to the west, and its shore is the lowest land-based elevation on Earth. It is about 304 m deep and, with a salinity of 34.2% measured in 2011, among the saltiest bodies of water, so that macroscopic life cannot live in it. Its surface area fell from 1,050 km2 in 1930 to 605 km2. Asphalt for Egyptian mummification and, in modern times, potash have been taken from it, and the area is also a health resort.
dean-barrow: Dean Oliver Barrow was born on 2 March 1951 in Belize City, then in British Honduras, where he grew up. He attended St. Michael's College in Belize, took a law degree at the University of the West Indies at Cave Hill in Barbados in 1973 and a Certificate of Legal Education at the Norman Manley Law School in Jamaica in 1975, and later studied at the University of Miami.

He entered the legal profession in 1974, working with his maternal uncle Dean Lindo, and became a partner in Lindo's firm in 1977. He later founded his own firm, Barrow and Williams, with Rodwell Williams. Among its more controversial clients were Lord Ashcroft and his associated businesses, including Belize Bank and Belize Telemedia Limited.

Barrow entered electoral politics in December 1983, winning a seat on the Belize City council as one of a slate of nine. In 1984 he stood for the newly created Queen's Square constituency, defeated Ralph Fonseca of the People's United Party and joined the first cabinet of Manuel Esquivel as attorney-general and minister of foreign affairs. He held his seat in 1989, when his party lost power, and became deputy leader in 1990 after the death of Curl Thompson. Back in government in 1993, he added the ministry of national security to his former posts; his detractors called him Minister of Everything.

In the heavy defeat of 1998 he was one of only three party candidates to win, and he replaced the defeated Esquivel as party leader and Leader of the Opposition. The general election of 7 February 2008 gave his party 25 of 31 seats, and he was sworn in the next day as the country's first black prime minister, serving also as minister of finance. He won a reduced majority in 2012 and a third consecutive victory in November 2015, which he said would be his last election as leader.

Citing his health, he at first intended to step down by the end of 2019, but on 18 November 2018 his cabinet urged him to stay until the general election of 2020, and he agreed. He did not contest Queen's Square in that election and endorsed his sister, Denise Barrow, to succeed him. He has returned to private practice as head of litigation at Barrow and Williams. His eldest son, Moses Michael Levi Barrow, a former rapper under the name Shyne, was elected to the House of Representatives in 2020 and later became leader of the party and of the opposition.
deeg: Deeg lies in the Deeg district of eastern Rajasthan, about 32 km from the city of Bharatpur, at an average elevation of 174 m. Its nearness to Agra gave it a part in the politics of the region. Deeg Fort is square in plan and stands on slightly raised ground; its walls of rubble and mud are strengthened by twelve towers, the largest of which, the Lakha-Burj, is at the north-west corner. The towers carried cannon. A wide, shallow moat surrounds the fort, crossed by a bridge on the northern side that leads to the only gate.

After acquiring the throne, the Jat ruler Maharaja Badan Singh chose Deeg as his stronghold and capital and began the building of a palace there, so that Deeg became the first capital of the Jats of Bharatpur. The town was almost constantly under threat of Mughal invasion, and his son Maharaja Suraj Mal ordered a fortress built to protect the palace. In 1804 both the Battle of Deeg and the Siege of Deeg set the British East India Company against Bharatpur's Jat rulers and their Maratha allies.

The palace complex served the Jat Maharajas as a summer retreat. It consists of several palaces called Bhawans set among charbaghs and water gardens, among them the Gopal Bhawan, the Kishan Bhawan, the Nand Bhawan, the Keshav Bhawan, the Hardev Bhawan, the Suraj Bhawan and the twin pavilions of Sawan and Bhadon.

The palace was in use until the early 1970s and now holds a museum. Its 900 fountains are run twice a year, at the Braj Holi festival in February or March and at a festival in September, and a fair named after Maharaja Jawahar Singh is held each year around September. Inside the fort a partly ruined palace, or haveli, of red sandstone is the principal building; parts of it were rebuilt in the 20th century. The 2011 Indian census counted 44,999 inhabitants.
delhi: Delhi lies in North India, spread chiefly to the west of the Yamuna river and bordered by the state of Haryana on the north, west and south and by Uttar Pradesh on the east. Two prominent features of its geography are the Yamuna flood plains and the Delhi Ridge. The Yamuna, a sacred river in Hinduism, is the only major river flowing through Delhi, and its floodplains are fertile but prone to flooding. The Delhi Ridge, which rises from the Aravalli Range to the south, reaches a height of 318 metres.

There are several legends about the origin of the name. One derives it from Dhillu or Dilu, a king who built a city here in 50 BCE. Another says the Tomaras used the Prakrit word dhili, loose, because the Iron pillar of Delhi had a weak foundation.

Seven cities have traditionally been associated with the region. The earliest, Indraprastha, is described in the Sanskrit epic Mahabharata as a city on a knoll on the banks of the Yamuna. The topography of Purana Qila matches this description, but excavations have yielded only painted grey pottery of the eleventh century BCE and no signs of a built environment or fortifications. The earliest architectural relics date from the Maurya period, about 300 BCE. The Tomara Rajput King Anang Pal built Lal Kot in 1052 CE, and the Chauhan Rajputs under Vigraharaja IV conquered it in the mid-12th century.

From the early 13th century until the mid-19th century Delhi was the capital of two major empires, the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire. It was a notable centre of the Indian Rebellion of 1857. In 1911 New Delhi, a southern region within Delhi, became the capital of the British Indian Empire. During the Partition of India in 1947 Delhi was transformed from a Mughal city to a Punjabi one, losing two-thirds of its Muslim residents, in part under pressure from arriving Hindu and Sikh refugees from western Punjab.

Delhi, officially the National Capital Territory of Delhi, is a union territory of India that contains New Delhi, the capital of the Republic of India since 1950. It became a union territory on 1 November 1956. The Qutub Minar, Humayun's Tomb and the Red Fort, all from the Sultanate and Mughal periods, are its three UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Delhi was an early centre of Sufism and Qawwali music, and its Khariboli dialect was part of the development that produced Urdu literature and later Modern Standard Hindi.
democratic-republic-of-the-congo: The Democratic Republic of the Congo covers 2,345,408 km2, the second-largest country in Africa after Algeria, and straddles the Equator, with one-third of its land to the north and two-thirds to the south. The Congo Basin occupies nearly the whole country and holds the Congo rainforest, the second-largest in the world after the Amazon, crossed by the Congo River and tributaries such as the Kasai, Sangha, Ubangi and Aruwimi.

Plateaus merge into savannas in the south and southwest, and the Rwenzori Mountains lie in the far east. The name is taken from the Congo River, which early European sailors named in the 16th century after the Kingdom of Kongo. Mobutu Sese Seko renamed the country Zaire in October 1971.

People lived in the area as early as 90,000 years ago, and the expansion of Bantu peoples brought major change in the first millennium BCE. Organised states emerged, among them early federated states around Pool Malebo, the Kingdom of Kongo, which ruled near the mouth of the Congo River from the 14th to the 19th century, and the Luba and Lunda Empires, which ruled between the 15th and 19th centuries.

King Leopold II of Belgium ruled the Congo Free State as his personal possession until 1908, using forced labour and concessionary companies to extract rubber, and violence, disease and exploitation caused catastrophic population loss. The 1904 Casement Report and diplomatic pressure led to its annexation as the Belgian Congo in 1908. Belgian rule continued direct control, racial segregation and forced labour. The Congolese National Movement under Patrice Lumumba won the elections of May 1960, and Lumumba became prime minister on 24 June 1960.

After the assassination of Lumumba and a series of secessionist movements, Mobutu seized power in 1965 and imposed a personalist dictatorship. His overthrow in 1997 ended the First Congo War, and the Second Congo War of 1998–2003 caused an estimated several million deaths and the assassination of President Laurent-Désiré Kabila.
The country has a population of about 116 million, with French as the official language, Lingala the most widely spoken of over 200 indigenous languages, and over 250 ethnic groups.
denmark: Metropolitan Denmark occupies 42,957 square kilometres and consists of the northern part of the Jutland peninsula and an archipelago of 406 islands. It lies between the North Sea to the west and the Baltic Sea to the east, and shares a 68-kilometre border with Germany.

Zealand, the largest island, holds the capital, Copenhagen, and some larger islands are linked by bridges, among them a bridge-tunnel across the Øresund to Sweden. The Kingdom of Denmark also includes Greenland and the Faroe Islands, which govern themselves under their own parliaments.

The earliest archaeological finds date to the Eem interglacial period, and Denmark has been inhabited since around 12,500 BCE, with agriculture evident from 3900 BCE. The Nordic Bronze Age, from 1800 to 600 BCE, was marked by burial mounds that yielded lurs and the Sun Chariot.

The first tribal Danes came to the country in the Roman Iron Age, from the east Danish islands and Scania, and spoke an early form of North Germanic; earlier, most of Jutland had been settled by the Jutes. The Danevirke defences were built in phases from the 3rd century, and the scale of the work in 737 CE is attributed to the emergence of a Danish king. Ribe, the oldest town in Denmark, was founded about 700 CE.

The unified Kingdom of Denmark emerged in the eighth century as a maritime power in the struggle for control of the Baltic Sea. It formed the Kalmar Union with Norway and Sweden in 1397, and the union lasted until Sweden's secession in 1523. The remaining Denmark–Norway endured a series of wars in the 17th century that ended in territorial cessions to Sweden. The constitution of 5 June 1849 ended the absolute monarchy. In the Second Schleswig War Denmark lost Schleswig-Holstein, and North Schleswig became Danish again in 1920.

Denmark industrialised from the mid-19th century and became a major agricultural exporter, and social and labour market reforms of the early 20th century formed the basis of the present welfare state. It stayed neutral in the First World War. A German invasion in April 1940 violated its neutrality in the Second World War, a resistance movement emerged in 1943, and the country was liberated in May 1945. Denmark joined what is now the European Union in 1973 but negotiated opt-outs, among them keeping its own currency, the krone. It is a constitutional monarchy with a unicameral parliament, the Folketing, and a population of over 6 million in May 2025.
detroit: Detroit takes its name from the French word détroit, meaning strait, because the city stands on a narrow north–south passage of water linking Lake St. Clair with Lake Erie; the French called the river le détroit du Lac Érié. The basin was inhabited by Paleo-Indian hunter-gatherers as early as 11,000 years ago, followed by Woodland mound-building societies, and at European contact it was a borderland of Iroquoian and Anishinaabe nations. In the Ojibwe language the area is called Waawiiyaataanong, meaning where the river bends.

The first Europeans to explore the river were a French expedition led by Adrien Joliet in 1669, and in 1679 René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle sailed Le Griffon into it. Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac and Alphonse de Tonty founded the fort in 1701. After the British took the settlement, Chief Pontiac failed to seize it in 1763, and the Royal Proclamation of 1763 set a buffer zone restricting European settlement south of the Great Lakes and west of the Appalachian Mountains.

The Great Fire of 1805 destroyed nearly all of the colonial buildings. The town was incorporated as a city in 1806, but the incorporation was repealed three years later, and it was reincorporated in 1815. During the War of 1812 it was captured at the Siege of Detroit and occupied by the British until 1813. After Michigan joined the Union in 1837, Detroit served as its first capital.

In 1913 Henry Ford's moving assembly line cut chassis assembly time by nearly 90 percent, and by 1920 the city's automakers were producing a million cars a year, roughly half of world production. The United Auto Workers was founded in Detroit in 1935. Decline began in the 1950s with industrial deconcentration and suburbanisation, and the population fell from a peak of 1.85 million in 1950 by more than 65 percent. In 2013 the city filed for bankruptcy, and it exited in 2014.

Detroit is the most populous city in Michigan and the seat of Wayne County, with 639,111 inhabitants at the 2020 census. It faces the Canadian city of Windsor across the river, and the Ambassador Bridge and the Detroit–Windsor tunnel connect them. General Motors, Ford and Chrysler, the three large car makers, are headquartered in the metropolitan area. The city gave rise to the music of Motown and techno, and its Art Deco buildings include the Guardian Building, the Penobscot Building and the Fisher Building. UNESCO named it a City of Design in 2015.
dhaka: Dhaka lies in central Bangladesh on the eastern bank of the Buriganga River, on the lower reaches of the Ganges Delta. The land is flat and close to sea level, and the city is bounded by the Buriganga, Turag, Dhaleshwari and Shitalakshya rivers, which leaves it susceptible to flooding in the monsoon seasons. The origin of the name is uncertain. It may come from the dhak tree, once common in the area, from the goddess Dhakeshwari, or from the dhak, a drum played at the inauguration of the Bengal capital in 1610.

Urban settlements in the area date to the first millennium. The region belonged to the ancient district of Bikrampur, ruled by the Sena dynasty, and under Islamic rule to the district of Sonargaon. Isa Khan and his son Musa Khan, who ruled from Sonargaon, headed a confederation of twelve chieftains that resisted Mughal expansion in eastern Bengal in the late 16th century. When the Ganges changed course, the earlier capital Gour lost its strategic importance, and Dhaka and Chittagong became the eastern frontiers of the Mughal Empire.

An early modern city developed from the 17th century as a provincial capital and commercial centre of the Mughal Empire. Dhaka was the capital of Mughal Bengal for 75 years, in two separate periods. It was the hub of the muslin trade and one of the most prosperous cities in the world, home to merchants from across Eurasia. The Mughals named it Jahangirnagar in honour of the emperor Jahangir and decorated it with gardens, tombs, mosques, palaces and forts. It was once called the Venice of the East.

Under British rule Dhaka gained electricity, railways, Western-style universities and a modern water supply, and became an administrative and educational centre as capital of the province of Eastern Bengal and Assam after 1905. In 1947 it became the administrative capital of East Pakistan, and the partition of India emptied the city of its Hindu population, which had come to form a majority during the previous century and dominated its economy. After the Liberation War of 1971 it became the capital of independent Bangladesh.

Dhaka is the capital and largest city of Bangladesh and the seat of its government. It has a heritage of about 2,000 buildings from the Mughal and British periods, and its most prominent landmark is the modernist Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban, designed by Louis Kahn. UNESCO has recognised the Bengali New Year parade, the Jamdani sari and rickshaw art as intangible cultural heritage.
diego-silang: Diego Silang y Andaya was born on 16 December 1730 in Aringay, then part of Pangasinan and now in La Union. His father was Pangasinense and his mother Ilocano. He was baptised on 7 January 1731 in Vigan, in the then undivided province of Ilocos, where as a boy he worked as a messenger for a local Castilian priest. Fluent in Spanish, he carried correspondence from the Ilocos to Manila, journeys on which he first saw the injustices of colonial rule.

Spain was allied with France in the Seven Years' War, and the British seizure of Manila in October 1762 inspired risings in the far north of Luzon. Silang at first wanted to replace Spanish functionaries in the Ilocos with native-born officials and offered to lead Ilocano forces on the Spanish side. The Spanish administrators instead transferred their powers to the Catholic Bishop of Nueva Segovia, who rejected the offer. The revolt drew on grievances over Spanish taxation and abuses and on Silang's belief that church and government in the Ilocos should be led by trained Ilocano officials.

Joaquín Martínez de Zúñiga, writing in 1805, gave a hostile account. He called Silang very quick and artful and said he persuaded the chiefs and many commoners, especially those of Vigan, that to keep the Catholic faith they must arm against the Spaniards and deliver them to the English. Armed men demanded that the alcalde give up his staff of government to the vicar-general; he did so and escaped from the province. The rebels then demanded of the bishop-elect, a Dominican named Ustariz, an exemption from the tribute, while Silang gathered troops for wider operations.

Silang was killed on 28 May 1763, aged 32, by a friend, a Spanish-Ilocano mestizo named Miguel Vicos, whom church authorities had paid and who was helped by Pedro Becbec. Gabriela Silang was forced to retreat to what is now Abra, led her troops towards Vigan and was driven back; she and her men were hanged on 20 September 1763, she last of all. The Philippine Navy has named two frigates after Diego Silang, one in service from 1976 to 1990 and one that entered service in 2025.
diego-velazquez: Velázquez was born in Seville, the first child of Juan Rodríguez de Silva, a notary, and Jerónima Velázquez, and was baptised on 6 June 1599. His paternal grandparents were Portuguese and had moved to Seville decades earlier. When offered knighthood in 1658 he claimed descent from the lesser nobility in order to qualify, though his grandparents may have been tradespeople. Raised in modest circumstances, he showed an early gift for art and was apprenticed to Francisco Pacheco, a learned teacher who encouraged his students' intellectual development. A contract of 17 September 1611 formalised a six-year apprenticeship.

By the early 1620s Velázquez had established his reputation in Seville. After the death of the court painter Rodrigo de Villandrando in December 1622, the Count-Duke of Olivares summoned him to court, and on 30 August 1623 Philip IV sat for him. The king was pleased, and Olivares commanded him to move to Madrid, his home for the rest of his life. He spent a year and a half in Italy from 1629 and returned in January 1631. For the Palacio del Buen Retiro he painted equestrian portraits of the royal family and The Surrender of Breda, his only surviving painting of contemporary history, in which the Spanish general stands before his Dutch counterpart as an equal.

He made a second journey to Italy in 1649, accompanied by his assistant Juan de Pareja, then a slave, and painted Pope Innocent X in Rome. He returned to Spain in 1651. In 1652 the king chose him as aposentador mayor, responsible for the court's quarters, an office that interfered with his painting. Las Meninas, completed in 1656, four years before his death, is regarded as his masterpiece.

He began in a precise tenebrist style and later developed a freer manner with bold brushwork. He used Caravaggio's realism and chiaroscuro only as a starting point, with a fluid handling of light and shade closer to Titian's. On his first trip to Italy he adopted canvases prepared with a light-gray ground, which gave greater luminosity and a cool, silvery range of colour. He painted directly from life. He is estimated to have produced between 110 and 120 known canvases, and no etchings or engravings.

His reputation languished in the 18th century, but by its end his importance was recognised, and in 1778 Goya made etchings after his paintings. In 1957 Pablo Picasso recreated Las Meninas in 44 variations.
doha: Doha stands on the Persian Gulf coast in the central-east of Qatar, at an elevation of about 10 metres, north of Al Wakrah and south of Al Khor and Lusail. Its name comes from the Arabic dohat, meaning roundness, a reference to the rounded bays along the coast. The climate is hot desert, with long, extremely hot summers, short mild winters and very little rain, mostly between October and March. Land reclamation off the coast has added 400 hectares of land and 30 kilometres of coastline.

Doha began in the 1820s as an offshoot of the older settlement of Al Bidda. The earliest documented mention of Al Bidda dates from 1681, in an account by the Carmelite Convent, and in 1765 the German explorer Carsten Niebuhr mapped it as Guttur. In January 1823 the British political resident John MacLeod visited Al Bidda to meet Buhur bin Jubrun, chief of the Al-Buainain tribe and the initial founder of Doha, and noted that it was the only substantial trading port on the peninsula. Written records often conflated the two settlements because they lay so close together.

The Al Thani family migrated to Doha from Fuwayrit shortly after Bin Tarif's death in 1847 and in the following years took control of the town, at various times switching allegiance between the Al Khalifa of Bahrain and the Saudis. Pearling became central to the economy, and the population grew to about 12,000 in the first half of the 20th century. In 1907 the city accommodated 350 pearling boats with crews of 6,300 men. That year the pearl market collapsed, and the aftermath led to the country's first custom house in Doha.

Qatar ratified its first constitution in April 1970 and became independent in 1971, when Doha was declared the capital. The University of Qatar opened in 1973 and the Qatar National Museum in 1975. In the 1970s the old neighbourhoods were razed and their inhabitants moved to new suburbs such as Al Rayyan, Madinat Khalifa and Al Gharafa.

Doha is the capital, largest city and main financial hub of Qatar, and over 80% of the country's population live in the city or its suburbs. Its population is overwhelmingly composed of expatriates, with Qatari citizens a minority, and most residents are Muslim. The metropolitan area includes Education City, devoted to research and education, and Doha Sports City, which includes Khalifa International Stadium. The city hosted the 2006 Asian Games and the 2022 FIFA World Cup.
dominican-republic: The country occupies the eastern part of Hispaniola, with the Atlantic Ocean to the north and the Caribbean Sea to the south, and shares a border of 376 km with Haiti. It is the second-largest country in the Antilles by area, after Cuba. The Cordillera Central is the highest range in the West Indies and holds the four highest peaks in the Caribbean, among them Pico Duarte at 3,098 metres. The capital and largest city, Santo Domingo, lies on the southern coast.

The Arawakan-speaking ancestors of the Taíno reached Hispaniola by around 600 CE, and by 1492 the island was divided into five Taíno chiefdoms. Christopher Columbus landed on 5 December 1492 and claimed the island for the Crown of Castile. In 1496 his brother Bartholomew built Santo Domingo, the first permanent European settlement in the Americas. Taíno chiefs such as Anacaona, Caonabo and Enriquillo resisted the conquest, but their numbers fell drastically from smallpox, measles and other diseases, and enslaved people from Africa were imported in their place. The last record of pure Taínos dates from 1864, though Taíno ancestry survived through intermixing.

By the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697, Spain ceded the western third of the island to France. A group of Dominicans declared independence from Spain in November 1821 but were annexed by Haiti in February 1822. Independence came in 1844 after the Dominican War of Independence, and the Spanish were permanently ousted in the Restoration War of 1863–1865. The United States occupied the country from 1916 to 1924. Rafael Trujillo ruled from 1930 until his assassination in 1961, and Joaquín Balaguer held office in 1966–1978 and 1986–1996.

The Dominican Republic is a representative democracy with an elected president and a bicameral Congress. Its culture has a European basis influenced by African and Taíno elements. Santo Domingo's Colonial Zone is a World Heritage Site and holds the first cathedral, palace, monastery and fortress built in the Americas. The name Dominican comes from Saint Dominic.
dresden: Dresden lies on both banks of the Elbe, mostly in the Dresden Basin, with the eastern Ore Mountains to the south and the Elbe Sandstone Mountains to the east. Because the river receives water from the Ore Mountains, flood protection matters: large areas are kept free of buildings as a flood plain. The original parts of the city lie in the boroughs of Altstadt, the Old Town, and Neustadt, the New Town, and historic outskirts such as Friedrichstadt and Albertstadt, built in the 18th and 19th centuries, are named after Saxon sovereigns.

Dresden developed as a German trading settlement on the south bank of the Elbe, established by the Margrave of Meissen, Dietrich, who chose it as his interim residence in 1206, the year of the first documentary evidence. A stone bridge built in 1220 linked it with a Sorbian settlement on the northern bank, later called Altendresden. Under the electors Frederick Augustus I (1694–1733) and Frederick August II (1733–1763), who also ruled as kings of Poland in a personal union from 1697 to 1763, Dresden became a major centre of court culture. The Zwinger, the Japanese Palace, the Hofkirche and the Frauenkirche date from their reigns, and the Green Vault and the Porcelain Collection were founded.

In 1806 Dresden became capital of the Kingdom of Saxony established by Napoleon, who won the Battle of Dresden there on 27 August 1813. The population passed 100,000 in 1852 and peaked at 649,252 in 1933. The American and British bombing towards the end of the Second World War killed approximately 25,000 people, most of them civilians, and destroyed large parts of the city centre. Dresden then belonged to East Germany, and after reunification in 1990 it became capital of the re-established Free State of Saxony.

Dresden is the capital of Saxony and its second most populous city after Leipzig. The Frauenkirche, destroyed in the war, stood as a ruin for fifty years as a memorial before it was rebuilt between 1994 and 2005. The Dresden State Art Collections go back to the collections of the Saxon electors in the 16th century. Carl Maria von Weber and Richard Wagner had works first performed in the city, and Coventry, also heavily bombed, became its twin city in 1959.
du-yuesheng: Du was born on 22 August 1888 in Gaoqiao, and his family moved to Shanghai the next year. By the age of nine he had lost his immediate family: his mother died in childbirth, his sister was sold into slavery, his father died and his stepmother vanished. He returned to Shanghai in 1902, worked at a fruit stall in the French Concession until he was dismissed for theft, and became a bodyguard in a brothel, and joined the Green Gang at 16. A friend introduced him to Huang Jinrong, the highest-ranking Chinese detective in the French Concession Police, for whom he became an enforcer in gambling and opium.

His rise came after Huang's arrest in 1924 for beating the son of Lu Yongxiang, the tuchun then ruling Shanghai: Du's diplomacy and money freed his mentor, and Du, Huang and Zhang Xiaolin became sworn brothers, known as the Three Tycoons of Shanghai. In April 1927 the three formed with Chiang Kai-shek the Chinese Progress Association. On the night of 11 April Du's lieutenant Wan Molin killed the labour leader Wang Shouhua at Du's house, and gang members wearing armbands marked Labor attacked workers and left-wing activists. Chiang rewarded him with the rank of major general and advisory posts.

From 1928 he moved into finance, founding the Zhonghui Bank and becoming a director of the Bank of China and the Bank of Communications. In 1931 he opened a temple to his ancestors; within months its private wings housed a heroin factory. When war with Japan broke out in 1937 he refused to cooperate with the Japanese, unlike Zhang Xiaolin, and went to Hong Kong, while Green Gang men working with Chiang's intelligence chief Dai Li smuggled weapons and goods to the Nationalist forces.

After the war he returned to Shanghai and founded the newspaper Shang Pao. He hoped to become mayor but gave way under pressure from Chiang, and in 1948 his son Du Weiping was sentenced to six months in an anti-corruption campaign led by Chiang Ching-kuo. In April 1949 he moved to Hong Kong, declining approaches from both the Kuomintang and the Communists. His health failed through asthma, and he died on 16 August 1951. He was buried in Xizhi in Taiwan, where the authorities raised a statue of him, though some doubt that the tomb holds his body.
dublin: Dublin lies at the mouth of the River Liffey in east-central Ireland, and its urban area covers about 345 square kilometres. The Dublin Mountains, a low sub-range of the Wicklow Mountains, border it on the south, with flat farmland to the north and west. The Liffey divides the city into the Northside and the Southside, and the city itself was founded where the River Poddle met the Liffey. The Grand Canal on the southside and the Royal Canal on the northside ring the inner city on their way from the west, both connecting with the River Shannon.

The name comes from the Middle Irish Du(i)blind, literally Blackpool, from dubh, meaning black, and linn, meaning pool. It referred to a dark tidal pool on the site of the castle gardens behind Dublin Castle, where the Poddle entered the Liffey. Old Norse Dyflin, Welsh Dulyn and Breton Dulenn all preserve the Middle Irish pronunciation.

Fish traps found during construction of the Convention Centre indicate human habitation 6,000 years ago, and others near St. James's Gate show Mesolithic activity. Ptolemy's map of about 140 CE gives what may be the earliest reference to a settlement nearby, calling it Eblana polis. A Christian ecclesiastical settlement known as Duibhlinn preceded the Viking settlement of about 841, Dyflin, which took its name from it; an excavation in Temple Bar has also found evidence of Anglo-Saxons there before 841. A Gaelic settlement, Áth Cliath, 'ford of hurdles', stood further up the river. The Irish government recognised 988 as the year of the city's first settlement, and Dublin marked its official millennium in 1988.

As the Kingdom of Dublin grew, the city became Ireland's principal settlement by the 12th century, following the Anglo-Norman invasion. It expanded rapidly from the 17th century and, after the Acts of Union in 1800, was briefly the second-largest city in the British Empire and sixth largest in Western Europe. Trinity College was established by Royal Charter in 1592 under Elizabeth I, and Guinness has been brewed at the St. James's Gate Brewery since 1759. After independence in 1922 Dublin became the capital of the Irish Free State, renamed Ireland in 1937.

Dublin is the capital and largest city of Ireland and its economic centre. The historic centre lies between the two canals, with O'Connell Street as its main thoroughfare and Grafton Street and Henry Street as the main shopping streets. The University of Dublin, the oldest university in Ireland, has Trinity College as its sole constituent college; the college was closed to Roman Catholics until 1793. Dublin City Council is led by a Lord Mayor, elected for a yearly term, who lives in the Mansion House.
durrani-empire: Ahmad Khan, of the Sadozai lineage of the Abdali tribe, was the son of Muhammad Zaman Khan, who had served as governor of Herat, and a commander under Nader Shah. After Nader Shah's death in June 1747 a loya jirga, or grand council, met near Kandahar for nine days. The two chief contestants were Hajji Jamal Khan of the Mohammadzai and Ahmad Khan. A holy man, Mohammad Sabir Khan, spoke for Ahmad Khan, reputedly placed sheaves of wheat or barley in his turban and crowned him with the title Durr-i-Durran, Pearl of the Pearls, from which the tribe took the name Durrani.

Ahmad Shah took Qalati Ghilji and Ghazni from the Ghilji and Kabul and Peshawar from the Mughal governor Nasir Khan. In 1749 the Mughal emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur ceded Sindh and the Punjab to save his capital, and Ahmad Shah then took Mashhad from Shahrukh Afshar and subdued the peoples north of the Hindu Kush. He sacked Delhi in 1757. In 1762 his forces killed thousands of Sikhs in the Punjab, in what Sikhs call the Vaḍḍā Ghallūghārā, and destroyed the Golden Temple at Amritsar, yet the Sikhs rebuilt it and he never subdued them. He died east of Kandahar in 1772.

His son Timur Shah Durrani took the throne in November 1772 and made Kabul the capital. Timur's sons fought one another: Zaman Shah, who succeeded in 1793, was blinded and replaced by Mahmud Shah in 1801, and Shuja Shah ruled from 1803 to 1809. On 7 June 1809 Shuja signed with the British East India Company the first Afghan pact with a European power. By 1818 the Sadozai rulers held little more than Kabul and the land within 160 kilometres of it. Kashmir was lost to the Sikh Empire at the Battle of Shopian in 1819, and Ayub Shah was deposed in 1823.

The army was based on cavalry armed with flintlocks, who made hit-and-run attacks. Its core was 10,000 mounted ghulams, or slave-soldiers, carrying blunderbusses; a third of them were Qizilbash who had served Nader Shah. The bulk of the army was irregular Afghan tribal cavalry armed with lance and broadsword, and infantry played a very small part. Ahmad Shah balanced tribal alliances and hostilities, a balance his successors upset when they tried to rule without the other Durrani chiefs. The Barakzai under Dost Muhammad Khan later displaced the dynasty at Kabul, and the empire is regarded as the foundation of the modern Afghan state.
durres: Durrës lies on the Bay of Durrës, on a flat alluvial plain between the mouths of the Erzen and the Ishëm rivers, on the Adriatic coast of Albania. The municipality stretches from the mouth of the Ishëm at the Cape of Rodon, across the Bay of Lalzi, to the Shkëmbi i Kavajës in the south, and the climate is a hot-summer Mediterranean one.

The area was inhabited from the Eneolithic, and from protohistoric times by Illyrian peoples. Greek colonists from Corinth and Corcyra founded the city in 627 BCE, on the coast of the Taulantii, an Illyrian tribe. A flourishing commercial centre emerged, and the construction of a Doric-style treasury at Olympia by the citizens of Epidamnos about the 6th century BCE suggests that it was among the richest cities of the Greek world. After the Illyrian Wars the Roman Republic made Dyrrachium its sole name.

The city became part of the Roman Empire and then of the Byzantine Empire, and the Via Egnatia began there and ran east across the Balkans to Constantinople. Its bishopric was created around 58 and became an archbishopric in 449. The Byzantine walls were built in the sixth century, after the Visigoth invasion of 481. In the late 10th century it passed to Samuel of Bulgaria; around 1005 his governor, Ashot Taronites, fled to Constantinople and offered the city to Emperor Basil II, and it returned to Byzantine rule.

The Ottomans ruled from 1501 until 1912 and renamed it Dırac. The city did not prosper in the first two centuries and became a den of piracy; its significance for the Ottomans lay in its castle and its salt deposits. After Ismail Qemali raised the Albanian flag on 26 November 1912, Serbia occupied the city three days later. It became Albania's second national capital, after Vlorë, on 7 March 1914 under Prince Wilhelm, and remained so until 11 February 1920, when the Congress of Lushnjë made Tirana the capital.

Durrës is the second most populous city of Albania, with roughly 2,500 years of recorded history. Its port is one of the largest on the Adriatic, with daily ferries to Bari in Italy. The Amphitheatre of Durrës, once seating 20,000, is the largest amphitheatre in the Balkans and is on Albania's tentative list for World Heritage status. The Durrës Archaeological Museum holds the mosaic known as The Beauty of Durrës.
dushanbe: Dushanbe lies in the Hisar Valley, at 750 to 930 metres above sea level, at the confluence of the Varzob and the Kofarnihon rivers. The Hisar range, which reaches up to 4,000 metres, bounds it on the north and east, and the Babatag, Aktau, Rangontau and Karatau mountains bound it on the south, so that it is an intermontane basin. The climate has hot summers and chilly winters, and the surrounding mountains shield the city from the extremely cold air of Siberia. Before the 1960s most of the city stood on the left bank of the Varzob, but construction later carried it across.

In the Stone Age Mousterian tool-users lived in the Hisar Valley. The Hisar, Bishkent and Vakhsh cultures, whose stone tools were found within modern Dushanbe at the confluence of the Varzob and Luchob, are thought to have inhabited it in the second millennium BCE, keeping cattle, farming and weaving. The area was later settled by the Achaemenid Empire, Greco-Bactria, the Kushan Empire and the Hephthalites, and in the Middle Ages by settlements such as Hulbuk, with its palace. Islam was introduced in the eighth century.

The town first appears in the historical record in 1676, in a letter from the Balkh khan Subhonquli Bahodur to Tsar Fyodor III, although the Balkh historian Mahmud ibn Wali mentioned the area in the 1630s. It was called Kasabai Dushanbe, the town of Monday, after a large bazaar held each Monday. Its place between caravan routes to Karategin and the Alay Valley, and to Afghanistan through the Anzob Pass, helped the market grow. It then had a population of about 7,000 to 8,000. From the 17th to the early 20th century it was controlled at times by the Beg of Hisor, by Balkh and finally by Bukhara, before the Russian Empire conquered it.

The Bolsheviks captured Dushanbe in 1922, and in 1924 it became the capital of the Tajik Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, which began its rapid growth. When the Tajik SSR separated from the Uzbek SSR in 1929, its capital was renamed Stalinabad on 19 October 1929, incorporating the nearby districts of Shohmansur, Mavlono and Sari Osiyo. The old name returned in late 1961 as a result of de-Stalinization. During the middle of the 20th century the city had a majority Russian and Eastern European population. Dushanbe became the capital of an independent Tajikistan on 9 September 1991, and the Tajik Civil War of the 1990s checked its growth.

Dushanbe is the capital and largest city of Tajikistan and holds most of the country's major hospitals. Its sights include the Tajikistan National Museum, the National Museum of Antiquities, Rudaki Avenue and the National Library. Its electricity is mainly hydroelectric, from the Nurek Dam, and its trolleybus system dates from 1955.
dusseldorf: Düsseldorf lies at the centre of the Lower Rhine basin, where the Düssel flows into the Rhine, and most of the city is on the east bank. It lies in the middle of the Rhine-Ruhr metropolitan region. Its name comes from the small river Düssel, with the suffix dorf, meaning village, so that the literal meaning is village on the Düssel. It reflects the original character of the settlement as a fishing and farming community on the riverbanks.

In the 7th and 8th centuries the odd farming or fishing settlement stood where the Düssel meets the Rhine, and the city grew from such settlements. In 1186 Düsseldorf came under the rule of the County of Berg, a state of the Holy Roman Empire. In 1263 the Count of Berg granted ferry rights to its inhabitants, and it gained city rights in 1288 after the Battle of Worringen.

In the Late Middle Ages and Renaissance it grew into a regional political and cultural centre under the Dukes of Berg and later as the capital of the United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg. In the 17th and 18th centuries it became known for its court culture and early art academy. During the Napoleonic era it was briefly part of the Grand Duchy of Berg. After the Congress of Vienna in 1815 the Rhineland, including Düsseldorf, was incorporated into the Kingdom of Prussia. The city lost its status as a capital but became the seat of a regional governor and it industrialised rapidly in the 19th century; its population passed 100,000 in 1882.

In the Second World War Düsseldorf was the location of a Nazi prison with forced labour subcamps and of five subcamps of the Buchenwald concentration camp, and the city's Rabbi, who had fled to the Netherlands, died in Auschwitz in 1943. The city entered the British occupation zone on 21 June 1945, and in 1946 it became the capital of the new state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Its population peaked at just over 705,000 in 1962.

Düsseldorf is the capital of North Rhine-Westphalia and, with 619,444 inhabitants in 2025, the second-largest city in the state after Cologne. It is an international business and financial centre, known for its fashion and trade fairs, and it has the largest Japanese community in Germany. The Kunstakademie Düsseldorf, its academy of arts, counts Joseph Beuys, Emanuel Leutze, August Macke and Gerhard Richter among its members.
dwight-d-eisenhower: Eisenhower was born David Dwight Eisenhower in Denison, Texas, on 14 October 1890, the third of seven sons of Ida Stover and David Jacob Eisenhower. His mother soon reversed his forenames to avoid two Davids in the family. All the boys were nicknamed Ike, and by the Second World War only Dwight still was. He graduated from West Point in 1915. In the First World War his request for an overseas assignment was denied, and he commanded a unit that trained tank crews at Camp Colt, his first command; he never saw combat.

He was promoted to brigadier general on 3 October 1941. In November 1942 he was appointed commander of the Allied forces in the North African theatre, in the campaign designated Operation Torch. In December 1943 President Roosevelt decided that he, not Marshall, would be Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, and he planned and carried out the Normandy assault of June 1944, Operation Overlord. After the German surrender he was military governor of the American-occupied zone of Germany, and he ordered camera crews to document the Nazi concentration camps for the Nuremberg Trials. He then served as Army Chief of Staff, president of Columbia University from 1948, and first supreme commander of NATO.

He entered the 1952 presidential race as a Republican, in part to block Senator Robert A. Taft, who opposed NATO, and won that election and the 1956 election, 457 to 73 in the electoral vote, against Adlai Stevenson II. As president he gave the Atoms for Peace speech to the United Nations on 8 December 1953, and in 1956 he signed the bill authorising the Interstate Highway System. After the Soviet launch of Sputnik he led the American response, which included NASA. Alaska and Hawaii were admitted as states in 1959. He died on 28 March 1969, aged 78.

His New Look policy relied on nuclear deterrence, building a stockpile of nuclear weapons and delivery systems to deter threats and save money by cutting expensive Army combat units. In his first State of the Union address in February 1953 he said he would use the authority of the presidency to end segregation in the District of Columbia and the Armed Forces, and when the services resisted he used government control of military spending to force the change. In his farewell address he warned of the dangers of massive military spending, which he called the military–industrial complex.
